p: Ellie flew on the second Saturday in September, at seven in the morning, in fourteen degrees and an altimeter of thirty point one zero, which was the closest Jordan had ever come to ordering weather off a menu.

Abby flew it from the left seat. Jordan sat on the right with the worksheet on her knee and Claire's weight written in her own hand, because Claire had stepped on Marisol's scale without being asked and then said, Don't read it out loud. Ellie rode in back next to Claire, on the booster cushion, in the lucky cleats, with Danny's cap held on by a hair tie looped through the strap. Biscuit came off 35R before the first taxiway and went up over the reservoir like she'd been waiting all summer to show off. Claire hadn't flown in ten years. Over the reservoir she said, mostly to herself, Huh.
Ellie didn't say anything for the first five minutes. Then she pressed her forehead to the window and said, to the window, She's not out of breath.

On the ramp afterward Ellie stood on the step and looked into the front of the airplane for a long time. Which one was Daddy's? Jordan pointed at the left seat. Ellie nodded like she was filing it. So that one's yours now. Then she hopped down and asked Marisol if she could weigh herself again, and Jordan stood there with her hand on the door for a while.
That was September. The rest of it was the pattern.

A text from Abby Strand. Next three weeks we live in the pattern. Takeoff, crosswind, downwind, base, final, land, do it again until you hate it, then do it until you don't. Tuesdays 7am, Saturdays 7am. Bring a sandwich, you won't get one.
Then, on the last Monday in September, a text from a number she'd saved in April under WALT (CLUB).
A text from Walt Herrera. Six months gone last week. Monthly logbook check tomorrow, before your lesson. I'll be at the fence Saturday.

No question mark. Walt didn't use them much. Jordan was in the station kitchen at the end of a shift, eating a granola bar standing up, and she read it twice. Six months. Thirty one hours in her logbook, every one of them dual, every one signed by Abby in green ink. Six months left to get a certificate she'd need, best case, all of them for. She didn't do that math out loud. Her partner asked who it was. She said the guy who wanted to buy her airplane. Her partner looked up from the coffee maker. Her airplane. She'd said it in her own voice, out loud, to see how it sounded.
It sounded fine. That was the strange part.
The club chat, meanwhile, had found something to fight about.
A message from Russ Kim. just noticing biscuit is booked tue and sat 7 to 9 for the next three weeks. by "noticing" i mean i wanted sat. jordan i love you but those are prime pancake hours
A message from Marisol Tran. She's doing pattern work. Six landings an hour. Biscuit's tires are mine for three weeks, Russ. Go eat pancakes in a car like a normal person.
Abby's Ground School: the rectangle, and everything around it.

Whiteboard. I'm drawing a runway, then a box around it, and I'm going to name every side of the box, and you're going to fly that box about two hundred times before you solo. Every airport in the country has this box. Once you can fly it here, you can fly it anywhere, which is the whole reason it exists.

Takeoff, and you're on the departure leg, straight out along the runway centerline. The AIM says don't turn crosswind until you're beyond the departure end and within 300 feet of pattern altitude. Crosswind leg is the short side, 90 degrees off the runway. Downwind is the long side, flown parallel to the runway in the opposite direction from landing, about half a mile to a mile out, at pattern altitude. You hold that altitude until you're abeam the approach end of the runway. Then power back, start down, and when the runway end is about 45 degrees behind your shoulder, turn base. Base is the other short side. Then final, lined up with the centerline, descending to the numbers. The AIM wants the turn to final done at least a quarter mile out. Upwind is the leg parallel to the runway in the landing direction, and you mostly meet it after a go-around.

Pattern altitude for propeller airplanes is 1,000 feet above the ground unless the Chart Supplement publishes something else. Ours is 5,885 plus 1,000. Call it 6,900. Look at what's on top of us. The Denver Class B floor over this field is 8,000. Eleven hundred feet of breathing room. You know how you found that out. The ACS wants pattern altitude within 100 feet and your speed within 10 knots, and I want it tighter than that, because 7,000 is the number that becomes 7,400 when you're busy.

Left turns are the default. In Class G at a field without a tower, 91.126 says make all your turns to the left unless markings or lights say right. In Class D, 91.129 says circle to the left unless ATC tells you otherwise, and ATC tells us otherwise all day. Here the tower expects right traffic on 35R and left on 35L, so the two patterns sit on the outsides of the two runways and don't overlap. Those parallels are only 700 feet apart. The tower people at Centennial asked the FAA to put that in writing for pilots: don't drift into the parallel runway's departure path on climb out, especially on windy days, because there might be a jet behind you on the other runway climbing faster than you've ever climbed in your life.

Coming in from outside, the standard entry is a 45 degree angle to downwind, aimed at the midpoint of the runway, at pattern altitude, level. The AFH says don't descend into the pattern, because descending entries are a collision setup. Here the tower will usually say something like "make right traffic, report midfield downwind," or give you a straight in, and you do what they said. 91.129(i) says no operating on a runway or taxiway, taking off, or landing at a towered airport without a clearance. 91.123 says once you've got an instruction, you follow it, and if you aren't sure what it meant, you ask right away. "Say again" is free. A runway incursion is not.

How the exam asks it. Know the leg names, the 45 degree midfield entry at pattern altitude, 1,000 ft AGL for propeller airplanes, crosswind turn within 300 ft of pattern altitude beyond the departure end, and that pattern turns are left unless marked or assigned otherwise.

91.113. Short rule, and the test loves it. First line: when the weather lets you see, you look. IFR or VFR, everybody's job is see and avoid. When the rule gives the other airplane the right of way, you give way, and you don't pass over, under, or ahead of it unless you're well clear.

In order. An aircraft in distress has the right of way over everybody. Converging, same category, about the same altitude: the one on the other's right has it. Easy check: if they're on your right, they win. Different categories have a pecking order. A balloon beats everything. A glider beats any powered aircraft. An aircraft towing or refueling another one beats every other powered aircraft, airships included. And an airship beats the rest. That's the whole list in the current rule. Think of it as whoever can maneuver least gets the most room.

Head on, both of you turn right. Overtaking, the one being passed has the right of way, and the one passing goes right to pass well clear. On final approach or landing, you have the right of way over aircraft in flight or on the ground, but you can't use it to force somebody off a runway they're trying to clear. And if two of you are approaching to land, the lower one has the right of way, but the lower one can't use that to cut in front of somebody already on final or to overtake them.

Here's what that looks like in Biscuit. High wing, so the airplane above you and behind you is invisible. The AFH points out the worst case is a low wing airplane descending on top of a high wing one, each of them blind to the other. Most midairs happen in daylight, in good visibility, near airports, below a thousand feet, between two airplanes going the same way, and the AFH says most of them happen on final or short final. Basically us, six times an hour. So you lift a wing before you turn, you look before you turn base, and you look at final before you turn onto it. Every time. That's not a style choice.
How the exam asks it. Expect two aircraft converging and a question about who gives way, the category order, head on and overtaking (both go right), and the landing rule with its limit.
The air a big airplane leaves behind.

Every wing making lift rolls up two vortices off its tips. Counter rotating, outward, upward, and around, and tight. The AIM says most of the energy is within a few feet of the core. They start at rotation and stop at touchdown, because that's when the wing is making lift. They're strongest behind an airplane that's heavy, clean, and slow. Clean means flaps and gear up, which is why a jet that just rotated and cleaned up is the one to worry about.

What they do next is what saves you. They sink, several hundred feet a minute, slowing down and weakening as they go, and they slow their descent somewhere below the flight path that made them. Near the ground, within 100 to 200 feet, they spread sideways at 2 or 3 knots. A crosswind of 1 to 5 knots can hold the upwind vortex right in the touchdown zone. A light quartering tailwind can push them forward into it. The AIM prints that one in capital letters, so I will too: the light quartering tailwind requires maximum caution.

So the rules are mostly about staying above and upwind. Landing behind a bigger airplane on the same runway: stay at or above its approach path, note where it touched down, and land beyond that point. Landing behind a bigger airplane that's departing: note its rotation point and land well before it. Taking off behind a bigger airplane: rotate before its rotation point and climb above its path until you can turn away. After a bigger airplane does a low approach, a missed approach, or a touch and go, give it at least 2 minutes. The vortices can be sitting on the runway.

Tower will tell you "caution wake turbulence." It's information. The AIM says whether or not they warn you, it's on you. When you accept "follow that Citation," you've accepted the spacing and the wake. Our Citations here land by the aiming point markers, about a thousand feet down. On a 10,000 foot runway, landing past that is free.

How the exam asks it. Heavy, clean, slow makes the strongest vortices. They sink and drift with the wind. Light quartering tailwind is the worst case. Land beyond the touchdown point of a larger landing aircraft, before the rotation point of a larger departing one.

Paint has rules. Runway markings are white. Taxiway markings are yellow, and so is anything that means hold or don't go here, even when it's painted on a runway. Remember that one fact and half the paint makes sense.

The big number at the end of a runway is its magnetic direction divided by ten and rounded. 35 points about 350 magnetic. Our 35R actually points 350, which is lucky for your crosswind math. L, C, and R tell parallels apart. Before the number, at the threshold, you've got the stripes, and the stripe count tells you how wide the runway is, eight for a hundred feet. Then the touchdown zone bars, every 500 feet. The first group, three bars, sits at 500 feet, before the aiming point, two fat white blocks about a thousand feet down. After that the bars keep going in groups of three, two, and one. Side stripes mark the edges. The centerline is dashes.

Displaced threshold. Somebody moved the start of the landing part of the runway, for a power line or a hill or neighbors. White arrows down the centerline in the displaced part, white arrowheads across the runway, then a ten foot white bar. That bar is where landing starts. The arrow part is still runway: you can take off from it in either direction, and roll out on it landing from the other end. You just can't touch down on it. Runway 10 here is displaced 400 feet. Land on 28 and you get all 4,800. Land on 10 and you've got 4,400. Yellow chevrons are different. Chevrons mean that pavement isn't for anything, not landing, not takeoff, not taxi. A yellow demarcation bar separates a displaced threshold from a blast pad or a taxiway in front of it. Yellow X's mean closed.

Hold short lines. Four yellow lines across the taxiway, two solid and two dashed. Solid side is your side. You stop on the solid side with no part of the airplane over the line until you've got a clearance. Coming off the runway, you aren't clear of it until every part of Biscuit, tail included, is past those lines. People stop with the tail hanging over the line all the time and then sit there feeling done. Right next to the line there's a red sign with white numbers. Red with white is a mandatory sign: runway ahead, or a place you can't go. The numbers are laid out like the runway: "17L-35R" means the 17L end is to your left. A black sign with yellow letters tells you where you are. Yellow with black tells you where to go.

Centennial has a sheet the FAA makes for this airport, with hot spots, places where people keep making the same mistake. Hot spot one: pilots told to taxi to 17L and monitor tower roll onto the runway without a clearance. Monitor means listen. It doesn't mean go and it doesn't mean call. You hold short, switch, and wait to hear your number.

How the exam asks it. Expect a figure of a runway with arrows, chevrons, or hold lines, and a question about what the pilot may do there. Know the sign colors: red and white mandatory, black and yellow location, yellow and black direction.

At night or in low visibility, the paint goes away and the lights take over. Runway edge lights are white. On an instrument runway the last 2,000 feet, or the last half if that's shorter, go yellow, a caution zone telling you you're running out. The light fixtures at the very end show red toward you on the runway, the end, and green outward toward arriving airplanes, the threshold. Taxiway edges are blue. Taxiway centerline lights are green. Flashing yellow lights where a taxiway meets a runway are runway guard lights. They mean the same thing the hold line means.
REIL, runway end identifier lights, are two synchronized strobes on either side of the threshold so you can pick the right runway out of a city full of lights. Runway 10 has them. So does 17R/35L.

The PAPI is four lights in a row on the side of the runway, usually the left. Two white and two red, you're on the glidepath, normally three degrees. Three white, slightly high. Four white, high. Three red, slightly low. Four red, low, and low is the one you fix right now with power. The AIM says a VASI or PAPI gives you obstruction clearance only within 10 degrees of the centerline and a few miles out, and you don't start down on it until you're lined up with the runway. Our runway 28 PAPI is only two lights. One white and one red is on glidepath.

The rotating beacon flashes white and green for a civil land airport. If our beacon is on in daylight, that often means the weather in the Class D is below 1,000 and 3, and you need a clearance to take off, land, or fly the pattern. Often. The AIM says don't rely on it. Use the ATIS.
How the exam asks it. Know the colors, the PAPI combinations, and REIL's purpose. The test likes "two white, two red" and the yellow caution zone.

Biscuit's com radio is older than me. If it dies in the pattern, the tower can still talk to you with a big light gun, a narrow, intense beam in red, green, or white. You need to know the table cold, because the controller can only tell you yes or no about what it thinks you're about to do.

In the air: steady green, cleared to land. Flashing green, return for landing, and a steady green will come later. Steady red, give way to other aircraft and keep circling. Flashing red, airport unsafe, don't land. Flashing white means nothing in the air. Alternating red and green, exercise extreme caution, anywhere.

On the ground: steady green, cleared for takeoff. Flashing green, cleared to taxi. Steady red, stop. Flashing red, taxi clear of the runway in use. Flashing white, return to your starting point on the airport. Alternating red and green, extreme caution.

Answer them. In the air by day, rock your wings. On the ground by day, move your ailerons or rudder. At night, either way, blink your landing light or your nav lights. If your receiver's dead but you can still transmit, the AIM says stay outside or above the Class D until you know the flow, tell the tower who and where you are and that you want light signals, then join the pattern and watch the tower. If your transmitter's dead, you can still listen, so monitor tower and watch for the light. Squawk 7600 either way. 91.129 says with a dead radio under VFR you can land if the weather's at or above VFR minimums, you can see the tower, and you get a clearance to land. With a dead radio, a steady green is a clearance to land.
If the radio quits on the ramp, you don't go. You call the tower on the phone, or you fix the radio. Usually the second.
How the exam asks it. The light gun table shows up on almost every test. The common trap is flashing green, which means taxi on the ground and return for landing in the air.

Wind almost never lines up with the runway, so you split it in two. The part along the runway is headwind or tailwind. The part across it is crosswind. Crosswind is wind speed times the sine of the angle between the wind and the runway. Headwind is wind speed times the cosine. If the angle is more than 90 degrees, the cosine goes negative, and that negative headwind is a tailwind.

True or magnetic. This is where good students lose points. Runway numbers are magnetic. The wind on the ATIS and from the tower is magnetic too, because they want you to be able to line it up with the runway. The wind in a written METAR or TAF is true. Here, variation is about 8 degrees east, so magnetic is about true minus 8. A METAR wind of 310 is about 302 magnetic. Use the ATIS wind against the runway number and you're comparing apples to apples. Use the METAR wind against the runway and you're off by eight degrees, which on some days is a knot or two of crosswind.

In the airplane you won't have a calculator, so use the clock. Angle of 15 degrees, a quarter of the wind is crosswind. Thirty degrees, half. Forty five, three quarters. Sixty or more, all of it. Like the minute hand on a clock: 15 minutes is a quarter of an hour. It runs a little high between 30 and 60 degrees and a hair low under 30. Close enough either way.

Biscuit's POH lists a maximum demonstrated crosswind of 15 knots. Demonstrated means a test pilot did it, in a new airplane, once, and it was fine. It's not a limitation and it's definitely not a goal. The FAA requires that an airplane be shown controllable in a 90 degree crosswind of at least two tenths of its landing configuration stall speed, and the number they actually showed goes in the book. Your number is on your kneeboard. Crosswind 8. Gusts no more than 10 over. Wind 15. Until I change it.
If the runway you're assigned is over your card, you don't fly it. You ask for another runway. "Unable" is a whole sentence. The tower will make it work or tell you to wait, and either one's fine.
How the exam asks it. Expect a crosswind component chart or a wind and runway pair. Check whether the wind is true or magnetic before you subtract.

Takeoff first, because it's easier. Line up, yoke turned all the way into the wind at the start of the roll. That holds the upwind wing down. Rudder to keep straight. The airplane weathervanes into the wind on the ground, so most of the time you're holding downwind rudder. As you speed up, the ailerons start to bite and you take some of it out, but never all of it. If the upwind wing comes up, you get side skipping, a row of little hops sideways, and that's how landing gear gets hurt. Let her stay on the runway a touch longer than normal, then lift off with intent, so she doesn't settle back while drifting. Once you're up, turn into the wind, level the wings, and crab to stay over the extended centerline.

Landing. Two ways to fight drift. Crab: point the nose into the wind enough that your track lines up with the runway. Easy on final. But you have to kick it straight with rudder right before touchdown, and too early or too late is a side load. Wing low, also called a sideslip: rudder to line the nose up with the runway, aileron into the wind just enough to stop the drift. Now you're flying a little sideways, on purpose, nose straight. The AFH recommends wing low in most cases. I want both. We crab on base and early final, then switch to wing low before the roundout.

Here's the part people feel in their stomach. As you slow down in the flare, the controls get mushier, so you need more aileron and more rudder to hold the same correction. Keep that upwind wing down the whole way. You'll touch down on the upwind main wheel first, then the other one, then the nose. That looks wrong the first ten times. It's right. After the nose comes down, ease off the rudder so the nosewheel doesn't steer you somewhere. Then keep adding aileron into the wind as you slow, until it's all the way over when you stop. The airplane is never done landing until it's parked.

Gusts. Add half the gust factor to your approach speed. If it's 14 gusting 20, the gust factor is 6, half is 3, and our 65 becomes 68. The AFH also likes partial flaps in a gusty crosswind, and so do I. Don't add the whole gust, and don't add it twice. Extra speed is extra float, and float in a crosswind is just more time to drift.
How the exam asks it. Crosswind takeoff begins with full aileron into the wind. On landing, the wing low method touches down on the upwind main wheel. Add half the gust factor.

Here's the most important thing I'll say this month. A go-around is a normal maneuver. It's not a failure. The AFH lists the two things that make people too late to go around: landing expectancy, which is believing it'll work out because it always has, and pride, which is believing going around means you did it wrong. Both of those kill people in good airplanes on nice days.

When do you go? Any time it isn't right. The AFH says if you aren't stabilized by 500 feet above the field, go around. If it comes apart below 300 feet, go around right then. Stabilized means on a steady glidepath to your point, on speed within plus 10 and minus 5, configured, trimmed, descending between 500 and 1,000 feet a minute, with only small corrections. Also: traffic on the runway, a bounce, a balloon you can't fix, a gust that puts you sideways, a tower that asks you to. You don't need a reason you can explain. You can explain it on downwind.

How. Power, attitude, configuration. Full power, smoothly, now, and carb heat off. The nose is going to want to come up hard because you're trimmed for slow and you just added a lot of power, and it'll yaw left, so you push forward and add right rudder. Pitch for a climb attitude. If you're very low, the airplane may touch the runway once. That's fine if you keep it straight. Then flaps up in steps, not all at once, so she doesn't sink back. Don't try to climb out of ground effect too soon, that cushion is borrowed and it gets taken back. When you're climbing, move over to the side of the runway so you can see anybody departing below you, and tell the tower.

Forward slip. You're high on final, and you want to come down fast without picking up speed. Power to idle. Lower a wing with aileron and hold opposite rudder so the nose swings away from the low wing and your path stays on the centerline. Lots of drag, lots of sink, no extra speed. In a crosswind you lower the upwind wing, because that's what keeps you on track. Pitch controls speed. The airspeed indicator can lie to you in a slip because of where the pitot and static ports are, so fly the attitude and the sound. Before the roundout, take it out smoothly. Let go of the rudder too fast and the nose swings and you gain speed.

Two cautions. Some POHs limit slips with flaps down, for tail airflow reasons, or long slips with low fuel, because fuel slides to one side of the tank. Read ours and do what it says. And slips are the best tool you've got when the flaps don't work, or the engine doesn't. A slip comes off the instant you don't need it. Flaps don't.

How the exam asks it. First concern in a go-around is power. Carb heat off. Flaps up gradually. A forward slip increases descent rate without increasing airspeed, and it's useful with inoperative flaps or an engine failure.

Tuesday, September 29, 6:40 in the morning. Walt was already in the hangar when Jordan got there, with Biscuit's logbooks open on Marisol's bench and his reading glasses on his head instead of his face, which meant he was done reading and waiting for something else.
Logbook's fine, he said. I'll walk out with you. He didn't say why. He stood by the tail with his coffee while she went down the checklist, and didn't say anything at all, which was louder.

She got to the left main gear and crouched. The tire had the usual flat spot shine from a month of landings. Turning it a little by hand, she saw it: on the inside shoulder, a strip about the size of her thumbnail where the rubber was gone and something white and stringy showed through, like the weave inside a bandage.
Walt was looking at the hangar roof.
A. Fly, but only full stop landings, gentle ones, to go easy on the tire until Marisol can see it.
B. Ask Walt if it's okay, since he's the safety officer and he's standing right there.
C. Ground the airplane, write up the tire, and call Marisol before anybody flies it.
D. Fly it. Tires wear, and this one's still holding air fine, so it's a squawk for after the lesson.

She writes LEFT MAIN TIRE, CORD SHOWING, INBOARD SHOULDER on the squawk sheet and puts the date and her initials on it. Marisol answers on the second ring, says a word Ellie isn't allowed to say, and shows up in eighteen minutes in sweatpants with a new tire in the back of her Tacoma. Walt holds the jack handle without being asked. I saw it yesterday, he says, while Marisol works. Wanted to know if you would. Jordan doesn't know whether to be mad. She decides she isn't, mostly. They're off at 8:05, an hour late, and Abby says the extra hour is coming out of Jordan's sandwich.

That's it. A tire showing cord is worn beyond limits, and the preflight is the pilot's last chance to catch it. Pattern work means lots of landings and crosswind side loads on that tire. Write it up, keep the airplane on the ground, and get a mechanic to fix it.

The ATIS said wind zero six zero at seven, ten miles, few clouds at one two thousand, altimeter three zero zero four, landing and departing runway three five right. Jordan called ground the way the FAA sheet in the briefing room said Centennial wanted it: who, what type, VFR, which way, and the ATIS letter.
Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, Centennial Ground, runway three five right, taxi via Alpha.

She read it back. Runup at the south end of Alpha, by the 35R threshold. Mags, carb heat, mixture, the door top latch, twice. She told ground she was ready for departure, and ground came back with three words: Niner One Echo, monitor tower. Then she rolled up to the hold short line for 35R, with its two solid yellow lines facing her and the red sign with 35R in white beside it, and switched the radio to tower. A Cirrus was on a mile final. The frequency was busy. Abby had her hands folded.
A. Taxi onto the runway and line up so she's ready the second the tower clears her.
B. Call tower: "Cessna Niner One Echo, holding short three five right, ready for departure."
C. Hold short on the solid side of the line, listen on tower, and wait for them to call her.
D. Switch back to ground and ask whether she's cleared to go now that she's at the runway.

She holds. The Cirrus lands. Ninety seconds later, without her saying a word: Cessna Niner One Echo, runway three five right, cleared for takeoff. She reads it back with the runway in it and checks the compass against the painted 35 as she lines up. Abby nods at the compass. Good. People hear monitor and go. That's the hot spot mistake. The FAA sheet lists it at 17L, and people make it at every runway end.

Yep. That's the one. At KAPA, "monitor tower" means switch frequencies and listen. It's not a clearance to enter the runway and not an instruction to call. 91.129(i) requires a clearance before entering a runway or taking off at a towered airport.
Off 35R she pitched for VY and watched the airspeed. It was a nice morning, the air cool and thick for Centennial, and Biscuit climbed like she was sorry about August.
At four hundred feet Abby said, Look out your left window.

Jordan looked. Runway 35L was right there. Closer than it should have been, even for two runways seven hundred feet apart. Biscuit's nose was pointed straight down the runway heading, 350, but the ground under her was sliding to the left. On 35L, a business jet was rolling.
A. Hold the heading at 350, since that's the runway heading tower expects her to fly after takeoff.
B. Turn crosswind early to the right to get away from 35L, then climb to pattern altitude there.
C. Ask tower if the jet on 35L sees them, and then hold her heading while she waits.
D. Turn the nose a few degrees right, into the wind, and crab so her track stays on 35R's centerline.

Five degrees right. The runway behind her stops sliding. She glances back and the centerline lines up again under her tail like a seam. Off to the left and below them, the jet goes up through a thousand feet faster than seems decent. Wind's from the east today, so it pushes you west, onto the other runway's departure path. That jet doesn't know you're drifting. Fly your line.

Exactly right. The wind from 060 pushes a departing airplane west, toward the parallel runway. The AFH crosswind climb uses a wind correction angle to track the extended centerline, and the KAPA tower specifically warns pilots not to drift into the parallel's departure path.
Fourth lap. Right downwind for 35R at 6,900, ninety knots, Biscuit trimmed and quiet. Tower had a lot of people that morning.
Cessna Niner One Echo, number two, follow the Cub turning right base. Runway three five right, cleared to land.
There was a Cub. Yellow, of course, a little shape well out ahead and below, slow as a bicycle, and getting closer fast.
A. Report the Cub in sight, slow to approach speed now, and extend downwind to space behind it.
B. Pass the Cub on the right like 91.113 says, then turn base once she's clear of it.
C. Turn base early and land ahead of it. She's lower and faster, and lower has the right of way.
D. Do S turns on downwind, without saying anything, to burn off the extra distance.

Cub in sight, Niner One Echo. Power back to 1,500, ten degrees of flaps on downwind abeam the numbers, and she keeps going past where she'd normally turn, until the Cub is on final and well ahead and turning base won't put her on top of it. Abby writes a little number on her kneeboard. It's going sixty and you were going ninety. Somebody has to change. It's always the one behind.

That's it. Following another airplane, you're responsible for spacing behind it. You're overtaking, so the Cub has the right of way under 91.113(f), and the tower gave you a sequence under 91.123. Slow down and extend to fit behind it, and confirm you have it in sight.
Seventh lap. The ATIS had changed to calm, and the wind on the field was doing that nothing that isn't quite nothing.
Cessna Niner One Echo, number two following a Citation on a three mile final, runway three five right, cleared to land. Caution wake turbulence.
Jordan found it. A white jet, gear down, settling toward the runway ahead of her base turn, sliding down a line she was about to join. She remembered the whiteboard. Below and behind.
A. Fly a normal approach, aim for the usual spot near the numbers, and just watch for bumps.
B. Stay at or above the Citation's path, note where it touches down, and land past that point.
C. Stay well below the Citation's path, so she's out of its way, and land short of where it does.
D. Ask tower for a little extra spacing behind the Citation, and extend downwind until she has it.

She stays a little high on the PAPI, three white, one red, on purpose. The Citation's tires smoke at the aiming point blocks. She picks the second set of touchdown bars beyond that and puts Biscuit down there, gently, with more runway ahead than she'll use in a week. Ten thousand feet of runway and a small airplane. That's the cheapest wake avoidance there is.

Yep. That's the one. AIM 7-4-6: landing behind a larger aircraft on the same runway, stay at or above its final approach path, note its touchdown point, and land beyond it. Calm winds make it worse, because the vortices can sit in the touchdown zone.

Saturday, October 3, 6:55 AM. The METAR on her phone said 31014G20KT. The ATIS, when she called it from the car at the gate, said wind three zero zero at one four gust two zero, runway three five right and three five left in use.

Walt was at the fence. It was a chain link fence at the end of the hangar row, with a view of everything. and He stood there in a canvas jacket with his hands in his pockets like a man waiting for a bus he didn't expect to like.
Jordan looked at the card on her kneeboard. STUDENT LIMITS. WIND 15. GUSTS NO MORE THAN 10 OVER. CROSSWIND 8. She'd done the math in the car with the engine off and the heater on.
Your call, Abby said. Show me.
A. Use the METAR wind, 310, against 35R. That's forty degrees off, so about nine knots across.
B. Ask for runway 28. On 35R the crosswind is about 11, over her card. On 28 it's about 5.
C. Take 35R. Fourteen knots is under the card's wind limit, and the gusts are only six over.
D. Cancel. A gusting wind is over a student's head no matter which runway they use today.

She shows Abby the numbers on her kneeboard. 35R: fifty degrees off, 10.7 crosswind, 15.3 in the gusts, which was over Biscuit's demonstrated number too. 28: twenty degrees off, 4.8, 6.8 in the gusts, 13 knots of headwind. Fourteen steady, six over. She calls ground and asks for 28, and ground says Niner One Echo, runway two eight approved. Expect a short wait. Abby says, Same airport, same wind, different runway, completely different day. At the fence Walt lifts one hand out of his pocket for a second and puts it back.

Exactly right. The tower picks a runway for most traffic, but you can ask for another one. With the wind at 300 magnetic, runway 28 is only 20 degrees off, so the crosswind is under the card, while 35R is 50 degrees off and over it. "Unable" or "request runway 28" is how you keep your personal minimums intact.
Decision seven. Hands into the wind.

Runway 28 was the kid sister. Shorter, narrower, the 28 painted smaller than the big 35s, and from the hold short line Jordan could see the far end, which on 35R you mostly took on faith. The windsock stood out full and leaned away to her left, and every few seconds a gust shook it like somebody had grabbed the end.
Cessna Niner One Echo, runway two eight, cleared for takeoff. Wind three zero zero at one four gust two zero.
wind from the right. then Compass checked against the paint Abby, conversationally: Your hands. Where are they going?
A. Turn the yoke into the wind halfway, then lift off early so the wind has less time to push.
B. Ailerons neutral, so the wings stay level, and steer with rudder until she's going fast.
C. Yoke turned full right into the wind at the start, easing off as she speeds up, rudder for straight.
D. Yoke turned left, away from the wind, so the airplane doesn't weathervane toward the right.

Into the wind. Yoke full right, on the stop, which feels like steering a parked car. Throttle in, 2,300 on the tach, which means 2,250. Biscuit tries to swing right toward the wind. Less left rudder than she'd figured. The engine's pulling left anyway. Airspeed alive. Forty, and the yoke starts pushing back, so she lets out a little. Fifty. Fifty five. She holds Biscuit on a beat past where she'd normally rotate and then lifts off with intent, and the second the wheels are free the airplane wants to slide left. Nose right, five degrees, crab. Over at the fence, Walt has a hand out of his pocket with some fingers up. A wave, she figures. For Walt, a parade.

That's it. AFH crosswind takeoff: full aileron into the wind at the start of the roll, reduced as the ailerons become effective, with rudder to hold the centerline against weathervaning. Hold it on a little longer, lift off firmly, then crab into the wind.

Tower worked them into the pattern for 28. On final, at about four hundred feet, Biscuit was crabbed a few degrees right, the runway sitting off to the left of the nose like a TV seen from the kitchen. The path ran down the centerline anyway. The two PAPI lights were one white and one red.
Okay, Abby said. Time to stop crabbing. Show me.
A. Add power and fly the rest of final a little faster, so the crosswind matters less.
B. Left rudder to line the nose up with the runway, then right aileron to stop the drift.
C. Level the wings and use right rudder so the nose points along the runway, letting the wind settle.
D. Keep the crab all the way down and kick it straight with rudder just before the wheels touch.

Left rudder. The nose swings onto the runway, and the runway starts sliding right in the windshield as the wind pushes her left, so she drops the right wing. A little. More. There. Now it's banked and pointed straight, and every instinct she owns says no. Ugly is correct, Abby says. In the flare it all goes mushy and she has to keep adding, aileron and rudder both, like turning up a drip that isn't keeping up. Right main. Left main. Nose. On the rollout she keeps feeding the yoke right until it's against the stop at the turnoff. Upwind wheel first. I want that one every time.

Yep. That's the one. Wing low method: rudder aligns the longitudinal axis with the runway, aileron into the wind stops the drift. With a right crosswind that's left rudder and right aileron. Hold it through the flare, touch down on the upwind main, and increase aileron into the wind as you slow.

Third lap on 28. Sixty eight knots, centerline, right wing down, and going well, which Jordan decided later was the problem. She started the flare at the thousand foot blocks and a gust off the right came through and lifted Biscuit like a hand under a tray. Ten feet. Fifteen. Nose high, 55 knots and unwinding toward the bottom of the white arc, and the blocks slid by underneath. 4,800 feet of runway, minus the ones already behind her.
Abby's hands stayed in her lap. Walt was at the fence.
A. Add a little power to cushion it and keep landing, since the runway ahead is still long enough.
B. Hold the nose where it is and let her settle back onto the runway. There's still plenty left.
C. Push the nose down hard to get the wheels back on the runway before the speed is all gone.
D. Go around: full power, carb heat off, right rudder, nose to climb, flaps up in steps.

Throttle in, smooth, all the way, Carb heat off, knob in. Biscuit's nose wants to climb the wall, trimmed for slow and suddenly full of power, and it takes a real push on the yoke and a lot of right rudder to keep her sensible. Flaps 20 to 10. Then up, as the needle comes around. She slides a little right of the runway so she can see down it. Tower, Niner One Echo, going around. The woman in the tower doesn't sound surprised. Niner One Echo, roger, make right traffic, report downwind. Halfway up the upwind Abby says, Best thing you've done all week, to the windshield, not to Jordan. At the fence, Walt has both hands out of his pockets.

Exactly right. AFH go-around: power first, smoothly and fully, carb heat off; then attitude, holding the nose down against the trim and adding right rudder; then configuration, flaps up in increments. Sidestep to see departing traffic and tell the tower.

Downwind, abeam the numbers, 1,500 RPM, carb heat on, flap switch to 10. Nothing. The indicator stayed at zero. Out the window the flap sat flush with the wing. On the panel the FLAP breaker stood a quarter inch proud of its neighbors, like a kid with a question.
Abby saw it the same second. Leave the breaker. You just lost flaps. Keep flying.
So she flew a no flap pattern without meaning to, and on final she was high. Both PAPI lights on 28 white.
A. Power to idle, lower the right wing, left rudder, and slip down to the glidepath at the same speed.
B. Push the breaker back in and try the flaps again, since a popped breaker is usually a fluke.
C. Push the nose down to get back on the glidepath, and let the extra speed bleed off in the flare.
D. Go around and fly a wider, lower pattern so she arrives on a normal no flap glidepath.

Idle. Right wing down, left rudder, and the nose swings off left of the runway while the airplane comes down like an elevator, wind roaring along the right side of the cabin. Airspeed needle all over the place, 60, 70, 65. Don't chase it. Attitude. Nine hundred a minute down on the VSI. At one white, one red, she rolls the wing up and lets the rudder go slowly, and lands no flap, flat, five knots fast, upwind main first. That's what slips are for. Flaps can quit. Slips can't. That afternoon Marisol finds a corroded connector at the flap motor, says it isn't her fault, and fixes it anyway.

That's it. With inoperative flaps, a forward slip increases the descent rate without increasing airspeed. In a crosswind, lower the upwind wing. Pitch controls speed, and the airspeed indicator can read wrong in a slip, so fly attitude. Take the slip out smoothly before the roundout.

Tuesday, October 6, the last week. Right downwind for 35R, clear and still. She keyed the mic to report downwind and heard nothing. No sidetone. She keyed it again. Then she noticed that the frequency, which had been busy all morning, had been silent for a while.
Abby flipped the radio to ground, then to the ATIS. Dead air both places. She pushed her own push to talk and shrugged. Old radio. Your airplane. What do we do?
A. Leave the Class D and fly to an untowered airport nearby where they don't need a radio to land.
B. Keep circling and wait for a flashing green, which means she's cleared to land.
C. Land. They were already cleared into the pattern, and that's close enough to a landing clearance.
D. Squawk 7600, keep flying the pattern, and watch the tower for a light signal before landing.

7600 on the transponder. Wide downwind, a mile out, 6,900, watching the tower cab like it owes her money. Base. Then a pin of green light from the cab, steady. Cleared to land. She rocks the wings, which feels like waving at a stranger across a parking lot, and the green stays on. 35R, rollout, off at Alpha seven, all the way past the hold lines. Flashing green: taxi. She wiggles the ailerons, feels dumb, and it works. At Hangar Six, Marisol unplugs the mic jack, squints, and holds up a green beard of corrosion on the tip of a screwdriver. Danny's coffee, she says. Ten years of him drinking it over the radio.

Yep. That's the one. With a radio failure in Class D, 91.129(d) allows a VFR landing if weather is at or above VFR minimums, you're in sight of the tower, and you receive a clearance to land, which can be a steady green light. Squawk 7600. In flight by day, acknowledge by rocking the wings. On the ground by day, move the ailerons or rudder.
Decision twelve. Every part of the airplane.

Saturday, October 10. The 7 AM weather: wind calm, 4°C, altimeter 30.18. Landing number nine. Sixty five knots over the fence, centerline under the nose, mains on about two hundred feet past the aiming point blocks, one chirp from the stall horn. Jordan knew before the wheels touched. Good, not perfect. At the fence Walt's hand went up, and she was too busy to count.
Cessna Niner One Echo, turn right at Alpha seven, contact ground.
Alpha seven came up on the right. She slowed to a walk, turned off, and rolled toward the hold short lines. Dashed side toward her this time. Solid side beyond.
A. Taxi until the whole airplane, tail included, is past the hold short lines, then stop and call ground.
B. Stop just after turning off the runway and switch to ground, since she's off the runway surface now.
C. Keep taxiing on Alpha to Hangar Six without stopping. Tower already told her where to turn.
D. Stop with the nosewheel on the solid lines, since solid is the side she's supposed to hold on.

She lets Biscuit roll until she can see the yellow lines go under the right wing strut, then gives it another length for the tail, then stops. Centennial Ground, Cessna Four Seven Niner One Echo, clear of three five right at Alpha seven, taxi to Hangar Six. Ground gives her the taxi. Abby doesn't say anything. She's writing in her own notebook, and she's smiling at it, which Jordan has never seen her do.

Exactly right. You're clear of the runway when every part of the aircraft has crossed the holding position marking, then you stop and contact ground as instructed. Leaving, you cross the dashed lines first, because they're on the runway side, and the solid lines last. They don't hold you on the way out.

She shut Biscuit down at the tie down at 8:40. Mixture to cutoff, mags off, master off, and the quiet came in all at once, the way it always did, like a door closing on a loud room. Nine landings that morning. Thirty one hours at the end of September. Thirty eight now.
Abby didn't get out. She pulled Jordan's logbook out of the flight bag between the seats, uncapped her green pen, and started writing on her knee. Sit a minute. I'm doing your book.

So Jordan sat. She reached into her flight bag for the green notebook. She'd been reading it in order again since August, a few entries at a time, and she'd stopped last week at a page with a coffee ring on it. She opened it there. For once she didn't have to go looking.

Danny's logbook, a page from October, nine years ago. October 14. KAPA, pattern, 1.1, solo. 290 at 16 gusting 24, landing 28 because I am a genius. Landings 1 and 2: fine. Landing 3: the worst landing ever done by a human person in a Cessna. Gust in the flare, ballooned, I held it there like an idiot because there was runway left, and she quit flying at like 10 feet. Bounce one. Bounce two (bigger, how). Bounce three I added power and sort of made it a landing out of spite. [cartoon: Biscuit drawn as a jackrabbit with wings, hopping down a runway marked 28, three arcs, each one taller than the one before, little stars at every touchdown. In the window, a stick man with his hair straight up. Over at the edge of the page, a tiny stick man behind a fence holding up two fingers. Arrow to him: WALT.] Walt was at the fence. He holds up fingers for your landings. That was a 2. He says he has never given a 10 and never will, it's "a philosophical position." Marisol checked the nosegear after and said if I'd hit the nosewheel first she'd have killed me, and I believe her. Lesson, in big letters so I see it: after the first bounce, GO AROUND. Go-arounds are free. Bounces are and also Walt.
She read it twice. On the second pass she laughed out loud, one bark, the kind that gets you looked at in a waiting room. Abby glanced over, decided not to ask, and went back to her pen.

Two fingers. Jordan looked out at the end of the hangar row. Walt was still there, collar up, hands back in his pockets, same as both Saturdays. She'd seen that hand go up after landings and filed it as a wave, the kind you give somebody you've decided not to like. She ran the mornings back like a monitor strip. A week ago, after the balloon, both hands out and staying out. And just now, the ninth landing, when she'd been too busy to count. Seven. She was almost sure it was seven.

She thought about the balloon on 28, and the go-around, and the half second when there had still been runway left and she'd let it go anyway. Nine years ago, on the same runway, he'd held it. She hadn't. She didn't feel smart about it, exactly. She felt like she'd been handed something, and had taken it.
And the morning they'd ended up on 28, twenty degrees off the wind instead of fifty. Danny picked 28 because he was a genius. She had the math on her kneeboard.
It had been a good three weeks. She could feel it in her hands, which had stopped gripping the yoke somewhere around the second Tuesday and started holding it.
She closed the notebook and put it back in her bag.

Abby capped the pen. Then she did something she'd never done in six months: she opened her door and climbed out first, ducking under the wing, and came around the nose to Jordan's side. She pulled the door open and held the logbook out, open to the page, so Jordan could read it.

Jordan's logbook, Saturday October 10. KAPA local, N4791E, C172N. Dual received 1.5. Day landings 9. Remarks: Traffic patterns, crosswind T/O and landings, go-arounds, forward slips, no flap landing, lost comm light gun signals, wake turbulence avoidance, runway markings. Ready for pre-solo knowledge test. Abby Strand, CFI (green ink, the S taking up half the box)
Pre-solo written is on the table in the briefing room. Pass it. Then next time I get out at the runup and you go around without me. She held up three fingers, the way Walt did at the fence.
Three. Full stop. Don't make it weird.
